classification.difficultyReason: Find distinct rectangular arrangements without counting rotations twice, then interpret patterns across the arrangements to formulate conclusions.

inlines.text: Six stars can be arranged in rectangular arrays in two different ways.
For this topic, 3 rows of 2 stars will be considered to be the same as 2 rows of 3 stars.

Draw rectangular arrays for each of the numbers from 1 to 20. Some numbers will have more than one possible arrangement. Use coins or counters to help you find the possibilities. What conclusions can you make about your arrangements?

answer.short:
Arrays, given as rows × columns, with rotated copies counted once:

$1:1\times1$; $2:1\times2$; $3:1\times3$; $4:1\times4,2\times2$; $5:1\times5$; $6:1\times6,2\times3$; $7:1\times7$; $8:1\times8,2\times4$; $9:1\times9,3\times3$; $10:1\times10,2\times5$; $11:1\times11$; $12:1\times12,2\times6,3\times4$; $13:1\times13$; $14:1\times14,2\times7$; $15:1\times15,3\times5$; $16:1\times16,2\times8,4\times4$; $17:1\times17$; $18:1\times18,2\times9,3\times6$; $19:1\times19$; $20:1\times20,2\times10,4\times5$.

Sample conclusions: primes have only a single-row arrangement; composites also have an arrangement with both dimensions greater than 1. Square numbers have square arrays. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite.
answer.worked:
For each number, arrange all the counters into equal rows. Try increasing numbers of rows, retaining only arrangements with no counters left over. Stop when further arrangements merely exchange rows and columns. For example, 12 counters form $1\times12$, $2\times6$ and $3\times4$ arrays; $4\times3$ repeats the last arrangement after rotation.

The completed arrays are shown below. Their row and column counts are factor pairs. The primes $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19$ have only the $1\times n$ arrangement. Every composite number has another arrangement. The numbers $1,4,9,16$ can form squares. One has only the $1\times1$ array and is neither prime nor composite.
